messages.subject: code alignment and static_cast<double>
parts:
[off issue, as this is more general]

> On Apr 27, 2016, at 6:09 AM, Michael Betancourt <notifi...@github.com> wrote:
>
> Many of the comments have been addressed. The only things that I didn't change were
>
> • I will get violent about having arguments aligned, even at the expensive of an extra vertical line. This will all go away once we have a decent logger, anyways.

My preference is the other way, but this isn't a big deal. Our code
format's not that well defined. We clearly differ tremendously in
our utility function for stretching programs vertically.

...

> • You can take my static_cast<double>s from my cold, dead hands. 😁 I can never remember which languages promote in which ways,
> so I tend to err on the side of being too conservative.

The usual code convention is to let the language do its thing
and not add extra annotation for readers who don't know the language.
And that goes for doc, too --- Google even says so explicitly in their
C++ style guide! That is, it's usual to prefer

a * b + c

to

(a * b) + c

and to prefer

int x;
double y = 2.0 * x;

to

int x;
double y = 2.0 * static_cast<double>(x);

At least you're not static-casting to var, which would be a performance hit.

> I'll keep this in mind if they pop up in the source code.
>
> In the future we should think about the virtual modifiers in base_hamiltonian.hpp. I had them there to define pure virtual methods to enforce an interface, but it might be fruitful to remove them to sacrifice enforcement for performance.

The only reason to have virtual functions is if you are going
to have references to the base class as arguments (i.e., you're
using object oriented programming). Otherwise, it's just a useless
performance hit. The compiler will let you know if you're missing pieces
of a necessary concept.

- Bob

Except that assumes the developer knows the order of operators
and promotion rules.  I’d rather start with safe code that’s faster
to write (because you know it’ll do what you tell it to) and then
clean it up later.

The only reason to have virtual functions is if you are going
to have references to the base class as arguments (i.e., you're
using object oriented programming).  Otherwise, it's just a useless
performance hit.  The compiler will let you know if you're missing pieces
of a necessary concept.

Well, until we get the final qualifier in C++11.

Yes, the compiler will err out, but trying to implement a concept
via compiler error is tremendously frustrating.  And any doc of
the concept then has to exist outside of the code, which is asking
for it to fall out of date, get lost, etc.

On Apr 27, 2016, at 6:33 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

Well, until we get the final qualifier in C++11.

How does that make a difference?

final tells the compiler that the current implementation 
is the final one (there aren’t any implementations higher
up in the vtable) so there isn’t a vtable lookup and you
get the same performance as if it the method wasn’t
virtual at all.  At least in theory.

has a reference to a base class at compile time. That is,
if you're actually using object-oriented calling patterns.
